Griffith John
GRIF-ith JON
proper noun
Welsh; Griffith from the Welsh Gruffudd, perhaps “strong lord” or “strong in faith,” and John from the Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.” Borne by the Welsh missionary to central China (1831–1912).

Biblical Definition

Griffith John, a Welshman set apart to preach almost from boyhood, was sent by the London Missionary Society to China in 1855, and for well-nigh sixty years laboured in the heart of that land, chiefly at Hankow on the Yangtze, planting the gospel where no missionary had gone before. He was above all a preacher and an itinerant, journeying through the interior provinces with the word of the cross upon his lips, and he poured his strength into rendering the Scriptures and gospel tracts into the tongues of the people, that the seed might be scattered widely by the printed page. Declining honours and calls that would have removed him from the field, he chose to spend and be spent in central China, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the applause of men. His life preaches the primacy of preaching in the Great Commission—that it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe—and the perseverance of a servant who counts not his life dear unto himself so that he might finish his course with joy. Broken at last in body and sight, he returned to Britain only to die, having given the whole of his manhood to a people who had no claim upon him but the claim of Christ crucified. The LORD is gracious, his name declares; and that grace was the whole spring of a labour that spanned two generations without turning back.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Welsh missionary who preached and translated in central China for nearly sixty years.

A Welshman (1831–1912), sent by the London Missionary Society to China in 1855.

A pioneer of the interior, planting the gospel chiefly at Hankow on the Yangtze River.

An indefatigable preacher and itinerant, carrying the word of the cross into unreached provinces.

A translator who laboured to put Scripture and tracts into the tongues of the Chinese people.

A man who declined honours and calls home to spend near sixty years upon one field.

Key Scripture

1Co 1:21 — "For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe."

Act 20:24 — "But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God."

Rom 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

2Ti 4:7 — "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:"

Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the primacy of preaching in the Great Commission.

expand to see more

Griffith John’s name is preserved not because any error has fastened upon it, but because his half-century of itinerant preaching rebukes an age uncertain whether the plain proclamation of the cross is still the ordained means of salvation. He staked his whole life on the answer that it is.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from his labour is the primacy of preaching: it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe, and men cannot believe in Him of whom they have not heard. His sixty years also recover the doctrine of perseverance, for like Paul he counted not his life dear unto himself, that he might finish his course with joy.

Hebrew Roots

His surname confesses that the LORD is gracious, and that grace was the root of a lifelong labour.

expand to see more

Griffith — Welsh Gruffudd, “strong lord” or “strong in faith.”

John — Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious,” the wellspring of his ministry.

Rooted in Rom 10:14—none can hear without a preacher, and he was that preacher.

Grounded in Act 20:24, counting his life not dear so as to finish his course.

A root in the foolishness of preaching (1Co 1:21) by which God is pleased to save.

Usage

"Cited as a pioneer preacher of the Chinese interior, chiefly at Hankow on the Yangtze."

"Named for a near-sixty-year ministry of itinerant preaching and Scripture translation."

"Held up as an example of persevering, self-forgetful labour that declined ease and honour."
